snippets.snippet_text: The Hebrew word for 'fasting' (tsum) traditionally meant abstaining from food, but Isaiah redefines it entirely: true fasting means breaking bread with the hungry, clothing the naked, and sheltering the homeless. It's not about what you give up—it's about what you give.

To 'draw out thy soul to the hungry' (Isaiah 58:10) uses nephesh—not just giving bread, but pouring out your entire being, your vital center. This is why Jesus echoes Isaiah when defining judgment-day righteousness: it requires a complete sacrifice of self, not mere charity.

When God responds to covenant prayer with 'Here I am' (hineni) in Isaiah 58:9, He's using the exact word Abraham used when God called him to sacrifice Isaac. Isaiah inverts the pattern: God makes Himself available to those who practice justice, binding Himself to their righteousness.

Isaiah 59:17 describes God arming Himself as a divine Warrior—putting on righteousness as a breastplate and salvation as a helmet. This exact imagery appears in D&C 27:15 and Ephesians 6:14-17, and it's the theological foundation for temple garments as 'the whole armor of God.'

In Isaiah 61:6, the entire people of Israel become 'priests of the LORD'—a radical democratization of priesthood that breaks the Levitical monopoly. This is the ultimate fulfillment of Exodus 19:6's promise that Israel would be 'a kingdom of priests,' realized through the temple endowment.

Isaiah 62:4's promise of new names—from 'Forsaken' to 'My Delight'—reflects how the temple is the place where identity is transformed. Just as Zion's shame is erased and she becomes the crown God holds in His hand, temple covenants replace our fallen condition with sealed, eternal identities.
